1:
What the word rendered burden signifies is explained by four of them. Calvin derives it from the verb to bear or carry, and says the prophets used it whenever they denounced some grievous and dreadful vengeance; and he adds a detail the others do not, that because they so often threatened the Jews with it the people came to call all prophecy by that name in ridicule. Wesley states the usage plainly, that when prophets were sent to denounce judgments against a nation or city the word was called the burden of that place. Ellicott renders it simply the sentence against Nineveh. Henry presses the metaphor hardest: this is not only a prophecy and a weighty one but a burdensome prophecy, a dead weight to the city, a millstone hung about its neck.

Two of them note what the prophet's own name means and set it against his subject. Keil and Delitzsch gloss it as consolation or comforter, and Wesley draws the point out, that a man so named gives notice of the destruction of their oppressors to the people of God, so that the comfort is theirs and the burden Nineveh's. On the prophet's birthplace Keil and Delitzsch argue a negative, that the town is not to be sought in Assyria at the Christian village on the eastern side of the Tigris, north-west of Khorsabad and two days' journey from Mosul, which some have identified with it; Ellicott refers the question to his introduction without settling it here.

Gill and Henry both set the prophecy against the earlier one delivered to the same city. Gill recalls that a prophet had been sent to threaten it with ruin for its sins, that the king and all his people humbled themselves and repented so that the threatened destruction was averted, and that having relapsed into their former iniquities they are now told their certain fate; and he notes the Jewish tradition that the earlier prophet was rightly said to have prophesied against this city. Henry dates the interval at about a hundred years and makes the same contrast, that the overthrow then foretold was suspended when the Ninevites repented and were spared.

The description of God that opens the prophecy is read by all of them as the ground of everything that follows, and by one of them as a deliberate inversion. Ellicott would render it that a jealous and vengeful God is Jehovah, an avenger, aye, wrathful, and observes that although several passages in the law attribute the same character to him, the model this prophet is following is a passage of opposite purport, the well-known proclamation of the divine attribute of mercy, which he is here reshaping. Keil and Delitzsch say the opening description has a double object, to connect the coming destruction of the Assyrian capital with the divine purpose at large. Gill divides the jealousy in two, for God's own honour and worship, so that idolaters must be punished, and for his people, whose injuries he cannot bear to see unavenged. Clarke glosses the terms one by one and dwells on the last, that though such men seem to prosper for a time and God appears to have passed their crimes by, he reserves and treasures up wrath which will burst forth in due time. Wesley grounds the vengeance in office rather than temper, since the supreme governor is bound to right the oppressed and to punish the oppressor.
3:
Ellicott turns on a single conjunction. The clause should read not that the Lord is slow to anger and great in power but that he is slow to anger yet great in power, since the whole point is that his forbearance is not attributable to weakness. Clarke states the forbearance without the contrast, that God exercises much longsuffering toward his enemies so that it may lead them to repentance, and that it is because of this longsuffering that vengeance is not speedily executed on every evil work; on the second clause he says only that God is able at all times to save or to destroy. Gill puts the same forbearance into the history of this particular city, which had already had proof of it when it repented at the earlier preaching and the wrath was deferred; and he adds the warning that follows from the verse, that they must not presume upon it and conclude he will bear with them for ever now that they have returned to their former impieties.

What the storm imagery is drawn from divides them by degrees of confidence rather than by opinion. Ellicott is the boldest: to vindicate the divine power the prophet reverts, in the manner of other Hebrew poets, to the wonders of the exodus — the pillars of cloud and fire in the desert march, the quaking cliffs of the mount, the sea and the river divided at a word, and Canaan giving way at every point up to the mountains in the north. Clarke calls it probably an allusion to the passage of the sea and of the river. Gill takes it as certainly that, since God dried the sea when the people passed through it as on dry land, and argues from it that since wind and sea obey him there is nothing he cannot do. Calvin is the most guarded of the four: there may be an allusion here to the history described by Moses, he says, since the prophets in promising God's help often remind the people how he brought their fathers out of Egypt by a miracle, and as that passage through the sea was held in high repute it may be that this prophet is alluding to it.

Clarke sums up the effect of the whole description rather than its source, calling the coming of God from the third verse to the sixth dreadfully majestic, since he is represented as controlling universal nature — the sea and the rivers dried, the mountains trembling, the hills melting, the earth burnt at his presence, and the three famous fertile regions withering and languishing. Keil and Delitzsch render the same catalogue in their own version, that he threatens the sea and dries it up and makes all the rivers fail. Wesley picks out the flower of the northern mountain as whatever flourished on it, the blossoms that were its glory.

The strangest phrase in the passage gets its best treatment from Wesley, who turns it into a military picture. The clouds are called the dust of God's feet, and though he is surrounded with darkness, an army far off is nevertheless discovered by the dust its feet raise; so God will appear with great power marching against his enemies. Wesley glosses the whirlwind in the same key as that which bears before it everything standing in its way, and takes the way that God has in it for the methods of his providence.
5:
Whether the quaking mountains are the hills themselves or the powers they stand for is not agreed. Gill takes them figuratively, reporting that mountains signify kings and princes and hills large countries and their inhabitants, so that what trembles here is the several kingdoms of the Assyrian empire, whose hearts would melt with fear at the news. Keil and Delitzsch render the catalogue plainly, the mountains quaking, the hills melting and the earth heaving at his presence with the world and all that dwell in it, and Ellicott corrects one word of the received version to that effect, preferring heaves to is burned.

Calvin explains what the whole terrible description has been for. It was given, he says, that men might know that when they come before God's tribunal no one will be able to stand unless he is supported by God's own favour; and since the enemies of the church relied on their power and raged immoderately against it, the judgment is set before them so that they might understand an account was to be rendered to one whose presence they could not bear. Gill puts the same question and answers it flatly, that no creature can stand before such indignation, neither man nor body of men, neither Nineveh nor the whole Assyrian empire.

The turn to mercy at the seventh verse is handled by all of them as the counterpart rather than the contradiction of what precedes. Calvin states the principle: God is hard and severe toward refractory men and merciful and kind to the teachable and obedient, not because he changes his nature or puts on various forms like Proteus, but because he treats men according to their disposition; and he quotes the comparison that this glorious description of the sovereign of the world, like the pillar of cloud and fire, has a bright side toward Israel and a dark side toward the Egyptians. Clarke says the same in his own idiom, that in the midst of judgment God remembers mercy and mingles promises among the most dreadful denunciations of wrath, so that none who trust in him need be alarmed, since they will be discriminated in the day of wrath. Gill grounds it historically in the deliverance of Hezekiah and his people, whose enemy's army was destroyed in one night. Wesley glosses the knowing of them as approving, owning and preserving them.

At the eighth verse Ellicott again changes a conjunction, and again to reverse the logic. Where the received version sets the overrunning flood against the preceding mercy with a but, he prefers and, on the ground that God protects his afflicted servants and therefore exterminates their oppressor, so that the two clauses are one movement rather than two. Gill and Wesley keep the adversative and read the flood as the judgment overwhelming Assyria, Gill taking the means to be a powerful army and Wesley the figure of a flood overflowing all its banks. Clarke offers a literal candidate for the image, reporting from an ancient historian, on a bishop's suggestion, that the river overflowed its banks, deluged part of the city and overturned twenty stadia of the wall, whereupon the despairing king burnt himself and his palace with his treasures. On the darkness that pursues, Clarke and Wesley agree in reading it as calamity and desolating affliction, while Ellicott renders the clause that he shall drive his enemies into darkness.
9:
Whose affliction it is that will not rise a second time divides Ellicott from Clarke, and Ellicott names the reading he rejects. Clarke takes the clause of the judgment itself: there will be no need to repeat it, since with one blow God will make a full end of the business. Ellicott argues from the vocabulary that the word means Nineveh's affliction of Israel, being the same term used a few verses earlier for the trouble that came upon Israel from Nineveh, so the promise is that Nineveh shall not afflict Israel a second time; and applying the whole passage to the destruction of the Assyrian host he says he necessarily prefers this to the other possible interpretation, that God will not have occasion to send the stroke twice. Calvin reports a third construction still, that some understand the verse of the chosen people's own calamity, that it would not be a destruction because God would keep within limits — the prophet on that reading checking the petulance of unbelievers who exult whenever the children of God are oppressed as though it were all over with the church.

Gill and Wesley read the opening question as addressed to the enemy and answer it for them. Gill asks whether they think they can frustrate God's designs, resist his power and hinder the execution of what he has determined, and whether the mischief devised against his people can be believed to prosper; Wesley makes the identification explicit, that what they imagine against his people they imagine against him. Henry places the whole passage historically, taking these verses to point at the destruction of the Assyrian army under Sennacherib, which he reckons a part of the burden of Nineveh and a pledge of the destruction of the city itself about a hundred years later, noting that the prophet with whom this one was probably contemporary spoke much of that event.

The two similes of the next verse are turned to different purposes. Ellicott re-renders the whole, that they shall be even as bundles of thorn faggots and, even while steeped in their drink, shall be burnt up like stubble fully dry; he explains that dry thorn cuttings were commonly used as fuel and that the verse compares the victims first to a compact bundle of such faggots and then to a second material equally combustible. Wesley draws a further point out of the folding, that thorns bound together burn together and so help to destroy each other, and reads the drunkenness as men unable to help themselves, the Assyrians being drunk with pleasure and pride and so easily surprised and overthrown.

Clarke takes the folding quite differently, not of a faggot but of counsel: however united their counsels may be, they shall be as drunken men, perplexed and unsteady in all their resolutions, and before the judgments of God they shall be as dry thorns before a devouring fire. Gill keeps closest to the imagery of worthlessness, that they are like thorns useless and unprofitable, harmful and pernicious, fit only for burning and, being bundled together, already prepared for it, so that the figure speaks not only of their character and their danger but of the certainty of their ruin. Keil and Delitzsch render the sequence without comment and carry it straight on to the wicked counsellor who is named next.
11:
Who is meant by the one that comes out is agreed on, but Ellicott pauses over how the clause should be construed. Another possible rendering, he notes, would make it say that the man has retired from Jerusalem rather than come out of Nineveh; he prefers the received version and regards the verse as addressed to Nineveh, and adds that what follows is plain enough to identify the enemy with Sennacherib. Gill gives the same identification, taking the man to be either the king who had his royal seat there or the officer sent from him with a railing and blaspheming message to Jerusalem, and Wesley names the same two. Clarke widens the reference to a succession of Assyrian invaders, listing four kings who imagined evil against the Lord before settling on the last of them and his spokesman as the wicked counsellor.

The next verse is where Ellicott's rendering does most work. Where the received version has the enemy quiet and likewise many, he would read that though they be of unimpaired strength and ever so numerous, yet just in that state shall they be cut down and the evil counsellor shall pass away; and he draws the point from it, that destruction comes upon the Assyrian army in the very hour of its prosperity. Calvin reaches the same sense by another road, saying the prophet is making clearer what might have been doubtful, that whatever strength there was in the Assyrians could not resist the coming of God's vengeance; Nineveh promised itself a tranquil state because it was well fortified and had a wide empire, and the prophet's point is that this security shall be no impediment to the hand of God being stretched out against it.

Gill reads the same words of the besieging army rather than of the empire, as men quiet and secure before Jerusalem who feared no sally from the besieged because they were so numerous, and who therefore betook themselves to sleep and rest. Clarke supplies the numbers, that the invasion was made with an army of nearly two hundred thousand, and that of these a hundred and eighty-five thousand were slain in a single night by what he describes as a suffocating wind; Wesley names the agent as the angel of the Lord and reads the cutting down as irresistible, sudden and universal.

The turn at the end of the verse is read by two of them as the closing of an account. Ellicott renders it that though God has afflicted Jerusalem he will afflict her no more, and Wesley makes the address direct, that God will no more use that rod upon Israel. Gill applies the whole to the same deliverance and treats the passing through as the stroke by which the besiegers were removed, so that what had been a threat to the city becomes the occasion of its release.
13:
The breaking of the yoke is referred by all of them to the same relief. Gill identifies it as the Assyrian yoke lifted from the Jews, who had been obliged to pay tribute or send presents since the days of Ahaz and were in bondage while shut up and besieged, the country around being laid under contribution, and who were delivered when that army was destroyed. Clarke names the tribute specifically as what is meant. Ellicott sets beside it the almost identical promise of an earlier prophet, that God would break the Assyrian in his land and tread him under foot on his mountain, so that the yoke should depart from off them and the burden from off their shoulders. Keil and Delitzsch render the sentence with the bursting of the bonds and carry straight on into the commandment given concerning the enemy.

The threat that no more of his name shall be sown is understood as a sentence on the royal line, and one of them tracks its fulfilment. Ellicott begins with a point of style, that sudden changes of person are a common feature of Hebrew poetry and that the denunciation here passes from the third person to the second; on that footing Sennacherib is told that the royal line of Nineveh is to be suddenly exterminated, a prediction Ellicott takes to have been accomplished when the last king of that city, his own great-grandson, destroyed himself in despair. Wesley reads the address as taking in both the king and the whole kingdom, so that none shall bear his name and title and the kingdom itself shall be swallowed up. Gill has the words directed to the king, following the Targum and the rabbinic commentators, and takes them for the decree of God concerning him and the ordering of providence toward him.

Clarke reads the clause about the grave as an address to the Assyrians and to their king in particular, and finds the manner of its accomplishment in the place where he died: the house of his gods was to be his grave, and it was while he was worshipping in the house of his god that he was killed. On the closing verse, Clarke observes that the language of the messenger on the mountains is probably borrowed from an earlier prophet, applied here to those who brought the good tidings of Nineveh's destruction, after which Judah might keep her solemn feasts because the wicked oppressor would pass through the land no more, being entirely cut off and the imperial city razed to its foundations. Gill localises the mountains, following the Targum, as those of the land of Israel or the hills about Jerusalem, and Wesley reads the two commands as one, that they should be careful to serve God and to perform the vows made in their distress.

Calvin uses the last verse to state what the whole prophecy was for. Everything predicted about the destruction of Nineveh, he says, was delivered to this end, that God might show by so remarkable an evidence that he had a care for his people and was not unmindful of the covenant made with the children of Abraham. Without that, the prophecy would have produced no wholesome effect on them at all, since they might have supposed that the overthrow of Nineveh came about by chance, or by some revolution of fortune, or through some other cause; so the prophet shows that the ruin of the city and of the monarchy was the act of the God who had bound himself to them.
